div.p: Large language model agents are increasingly used to analyze potential software vulnerabilities, but their outputs can silently violate domain knowledge, limiting their reliability in safety-critical settings such as medical devices. Prior work either treats that output as a prediction to be scored or constrains it to walks within a single knowledge graph; neither checks whether reasoning over a binary is entailed by an independent body of domain knowledge. We present EntailLLM, a framework that includes a specialized LLM agent and a validation mechanism. The agent proposes a traversal path of the function call graph for a vulnerability, which is checked against a separate knowledge graph and a logic program by an entailment procedure under annotated logic. We evaluate EntailLLM by examining six specialized agents across three CWE classes, and eight binaries varying in size from 405 to 12,696 functions. The agents improve pooled entailment from 77% to 98%, with entailment decreasing in only 3 of 118 configurations. We found that the best-performing agent combines self-refinement and a priori domain knowledge. EntailLLM is deployed end-to-end on real medical-device binaries, reaching 98% pooled entailment without per-device tuning. Our framework inherits the formal guarantees of generalized annotated logic, providing logical verification of agent output that is both explainable and grounded in well-defined semantics.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Language model agents are increasingly applied to vulnerability discovery, from detection and triage to exploit reasoning and patch generation [23]. Yet they remain unreliable at identifying and reasoning about vulnerabilities unaided [28], they produce confident inferences that probability-based checks cannot catch [18], and they mislead analysts when their suggestions go unchecked [5]. These problems worsen for bespoke reverse-engineering tasks in This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution International 4.0 License. domains such as medical devices, whose firmware is long-lived, hard to patch, and rarely shipped with source [7]. Analysis proceeds on decompiled binaries, where the semantic cues of source code are absent, and intent must be reconstructed from low-level structure. Yet analysts already use LLMs to decide where to look in a binary [5], and attackers increasingly do the same [8]. What such a model proposes is therefore both a prediction of how the code will be explored and something that needs checking for alignment with the domain knowledge.

We present EntailLLM, a framework deployed at scale on real medical-device firmware, that verifies agent-proposed paths against domain knowledge. We show that when that knowledge is used to guide the agent, its proposals are entailed more often. Figure 1 is a screenshot of EntailLLM catching erroneous LLM-agent output by flagging an LLM conclusion the domain knowledge does not support. The library function memset is correctly assigned to the memory-management class, but the LLM then assumes it can perform an integer size calculation-an inference that is structurally unremarkable yet supported by nothing memset does. The distinction that makes this possible is the difference between statistical clean-up: pruning candidate paths by structural signals such as the call graph, which an LLM or a graph-based method already arXiv:2608.01763v2 [cs.CR] 25 Oct 2026

Preprint, under review does well, and semantic clean-up: rejecting a path that violates the meaning of the domain even when it is structurally plausible. Our logic-based reasoner supplies the latter exactly, with a trace for every decision. Table 1 shows why the problem is hard in practice, where device binaries are often large. Without a neural model like an LLM, paths could be formed directly from the call graph under the same constraints. But enumerating them is intractable on large binaries (up to 2.1 × 10 6 direct six-edge call chains on unsafelib, growing about 2.4× per added edge), and a sample of them is entailed only about half the time (No-LLM column). En-tailLLM comprises an LLM-based agent that proposes paths, and a reasoner that treats each proposed path as a hypothesis and admits it only if a domain-knowledge graph (DKG) entails it. The path is a traversal of the binary's call graph while the constraints come from a separate DKG, so verification is an alignment between two graphs rather than a walk within one. The domain encoding instantiates hand-crafted schemas over the knowledge graph's triples, yielding conjunctive, co-dependent-label rules grounded in CWE, MITRE, and device documentation. Using an LLM makes the agentic search tractable by producing a manageable number of proposals from the binary's call graph, and the paths are entailed more often than in the No-LLM case (Unguided column). An LLM, trained to respond to various user requests in language, captures human-like intuition. However, we want the agentic output to align with the domain knowledge. We use entailment as a procedure to determine this alignment. If the domain knowledge is correct, we would expect an entailed agentic output to likely lead to an actual vulnerability. However, here we focus only on how to best answer the entailment question. We have ongoing work to evaluate the end-to-end system in terms of finding vulnerabilities. And this includes validation of the domain knowledge itself. In this work, we try to find an effective way to guide the output of a neural agent by providing semantic labels from a symbolic system. As shown in Table 1, guiding the agent with labels derived from the domain knowledge raises entailment further. The results show that symbols from a symbolic reasoner can guide neural generators like LLMs, and the neurosymbolic system performs better than a symbolic agent or an agent with an unaided LLM. To identify the most effective way of guiding a neural agent with symbolic knowledge, we evaluate our framework for six agents across several LLM models, binaries, and three different CWEs. We find that adding domain knowledge with a self-refinement prompting strategy raises the fraction of paths entailed from 71% to 97% while increasing the number of entailed paths by 31%, from 1,297 to 1,705, over all three Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) classes.

Our contributions are: (i) a neurosymbolic approach to agentic binary analysis in which domain knowledge guides an agent's proposed paths through code, and a symbolic reasoner checks if those paths are entailed; (ii) a deployed, end-to-end system that localizes and explains non-entailments, reporting the first unsupported step with the rule firings behind it; and (iii) an evaluation of six agents across three CWE classes, four LLMs, and eight binaries, in which guidance from domain knowledge raises pooled entailment across agents from 77% to 98%, decreasing in only 3 of 118 configurations, and the gain persists when guidance and verification use disjoint halves of the knowledge graph. Related Work. Work that reports gains from LLMs on security tasks pairs the model with structure rather than trusting it alone [12].

Applying LLMs directly to stripped or decompiled binaries recovers source-like code, symbols, and readable decompiler output [9,26,31], improving the representation an analyst works from but not verifying that reasoning over it is consistent with what is known about the vulnerability class. Other work gates LLMs with structure to similar ends, translating a problem into symbolic form for a solver [18] or constraining generation to paths grounded in a knowledge graph [14,15] or letting an LLM agent beam-search a knowledge graph for reasoning paths [25]. These align reasoning to a walk within a single KG and are evaluated on natural-language QA. Our arrangement is closest to shielding in safe reinforcement learning [2] and to logic-based LLM guardrails [10], where the agent proposes freely, and the logic decides what passes. But a shield strong enough to block unsafe behavior typically blocks useful behavior with it. Here we show that enriching the generator with the domain knowledge's own derived vocabulary raises the entailed rate more than shielding alone and the count as well for the agent following a self-refinement strategy. Classical taint-based discovery and its recent LLM-driven variants [13,19] share our binary-level, source-free setting but aim to emit vulnerability alerts; where they use the LLM to produce the analysis, we use logic to check it. A detailed literature review appears in the Appendix.

div.head: Problem Description
div.p: Technical Preliminaries. We reason in generalized annotated logic [11], which supplies a single formal semantics generalizing fuzzy and other real-valued logics, and we work in a tractable fragment that admits exact polynomial-time deduction [21] and represents time explicitly [22]. We recall only what is needed here and refer the reader to that work for the full development. An annotated literal 𝑎:𝜇 pairs a literal with an annotation 𝜇 = [ℓ, 𝑢] ⊆ [0, 1]. The lattice is ordered so that [0, 1]-total uncertainty-is the bottom element, while tight intervals such as [1, 1] and [0, 0] sit at the top. This makes the logic open-world: an unobserved literal is not false but merely uncertain, and inference narrows it, so the partial and noisy observations recovered from a binary need not be forced to true or false. A temporal annotated fact (TAF) asserts such a literal at a time point, written 𝑎:(𝜇, 𝑡), and rules take the form

where a body, defined as a conjunct in the standard way, satisfied at 𝑡 makes the head hold at 𝑡 + Δ𝑡. A program Π is a set of TAFs and rules. An interpretation 𝐼 maps each ground literal and time point to an annotation; it satisfies 𝑎:𝜇 at 𝑡 when 𝜇 ⊑ 𝐼 (𝑎, 𝑡), and is a model of Π when it satisfies every rule and TAF. Deduction iterates a fixpoint operator Γ to convergence, yielding the minimal model 𝐼 * . Γ is monotonic, converges in polynomial number of applications, and decides entailment. Entailment is therefore an exact, decidable consequence of the program's semantics rather than a heuristic score, and because every interpretation is produced by an identifiable rule firing, each inference carries a trace of the facts and rules that led to it. Entailment Checking Agent Paths. Given a target binary and a weakness class (CWE), the agent predicts exploration workflows a human analyst might follow through the binary's functions toward a vulnerability of that class. Weakness classes come from the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) maintained by MITRE [27]. The NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) [17] catalogues publicly disclosed vulnerabilities (CVEs) and maps them to CWE weakness types. The input is the binary's function call graph, functions as nodes and calls as edges, with each function labeled with a set of libc labels; the output is a sequence of call-graph nodes, each reachable from the previous one within a few call edges. Our prompts steer exploration toward the target weakness class, and entailed traversals feed a fuzzer downstream in the deployed system, so the traversal is the input to discovery rather than a substitute for it. We evaluate CWE-121 (stack-based buffer overflow), CWE-415 (double free), and CWE-416 (use-after-free). The agent performs a standard beam search over LLM outputs to check for paths realizable in a given binary. The logical verification step is only applied after that, to check if such a path adheres to domain knowledge. We first fix a domain-knowledge program Π = Π 𝑇 𝐴𝐹𝑠 ∪ Π 𝑅𝑢𝑙𝑒𝑠 , whose facts encode the DKG and whose rules are described in Section 3. We denote a sequence of code blocks, that is, the binary's functions, the nodes of its call graph, as: 𝜏 = ⟨𝐶𝐵 0 , . . . , 𝐶𝐵 𝑛 ⟩. Then a candidate trajectory generated by an agent linked by a predicate called stepFrom is encoded by TAFs, and can be written as (Theorems 3.2 and 3.4 of [20]), this decision and the localization of 𝑖 * are exact rather than heuristic. We focused development on binary analysis because of our target deployment; the framework itself is agnostic to whether the call graph and its labels come from a decompiler or from source, and we leave source-code analysis to future work, studying a complete binary pipeline here. Several domain-specific reasons motivate the choice. Device firmware ships without source, and the compiled artifact is what runs, and optimization and field patching can leave it diverging from any source tree. We consume decompiler output rather than raw bytes because the decompiler recovers the call graph and, from symbol and relocation tables, the imported libc calls we use as labels-beacons that survive stripping, so no debug information is needed. We verify all traversals rather than only paths terminating in a vulnerability. Reverse engineers proceed by beacon-driven exploration, recognizing API calls, strings, and constants to form and test hypotheses [6,24,29], so restricting attention to vulnerability terminating paths would discard the exploratory structure that makes the output useful and presuppose the analyst's conclusion. Finally, admitting only domain-entailed paths reduces the volume of unsupported paths a human must triage and yields explainable traces an auditor can inspect. Entailment measures conformance to the encoded domain knowledge. Our problem setting is defensive in nature. We want to predict how an analyst might approach a codebase, and identify which type of agent yields the exploration most consistent with domain knowledge.

div.head: System description
div.p: Figure 2 shows the EntailLLM framework within an end-to-end cybersecurity pipeline. The input to the system is the analyzed binary's call graph together with the libc labels of its functions. From these inputs, EntailLLM proceeds through two core stages: agentic path generation and logical verification, before emitting the paths that survive verification. Labeled call graph. In our experiment, we use Ghidra's static analysis to recover the binary's structural representation. It disassembles the machine code, reconstructs functions and their boundaries, produces decompiled C-like output, and recovers the interprocedural call graph with cross-references. From symbol and relocation information, it resolves the names of imported libc functions (e.g., strcpy, gets, realloc, system), yielding for each function in the call graph the set of libc calls it references. Selecting a path from this graph without a parsimony requirement leads to arbitrary outcomes. Evaluating them all is intractable. In our agent, we leverage an LLM's documented capability for searching for potential vulnerability discovery as a parsimony requirement. Domain Knowledge (DK). DK is a CWE-focused, code-centric ontology together with instantiated knowledge graphs for CWE-121, CWE-415, and CWE-416. We note that our approach is agnostic to the underlying knowledge graph, and it does not necessarily have to be associated with a CWE. Ablation studies in section 4.2 show the utility of our method irrespective of the domain knowledge. The ontology used defines a layered class hierarchy, from concrete beacons, code entities, code operations, and code patterns, to fault conditions and outcome-level faults and CWE-level vulnerability classes. They are connected by typed relations such as is_a, can_cause, and mitigates. Each graph is populated by automated extraction from technical corpora (reverse-engineering manuals, security advisories, man pages), then refined by schema validation with targeted semantic review; together they span 105-188 entities and 232-403 relations over 14-16 relation types (pergraph counts in Appendix). A central modeling choice represents faults as unsafe variants of otherwise-neutral operations; for example, an out_of_bounds_write is an unsafe_variant_of a generic memory_write. Safe and unsafe behavior coexist in one graph, and the reasoner can express how missing validation turns an ordinary operation into a memory-corruption event. DK also supplies the mapping rules that lift raw libc labels onto its own vocabulary during reasoning, so the labels attached to functions are expressed in the terms against which paths are later checked for entailment. For the guided agents (+DK experimental setting), we pre-run a single inference step over the call graph, with only rules that derive high-level concept labels for each function. These labels are then appended to that function's label group in the prompt, before any path is generated. The model receives only these per-function labels, never the knowledge graph's relations or the traversal rules that decide entailment. We hypothesize that making semantically meaningful domain knowledge labels available to the agent would improve the proposed paths. Viewed another way, by adding domain knowledge in the LLM prompt, we aim to bias the conditional probability of generated tokens towards an entailed solution. As labels come from the same graph that the verifier reasons with, in Section 4.2 we split each graph into two disjoint halves, guide generation with one and verify with the other. We find that the half that never supplied a path's labels entails it about as often as the half that did, showing no sign of circularity or leakage. Instead, if we added the whole domain knowledge in the context window, it would leak the graph relations to the generator, turning path proposal into a lookup of transitions the verifier already accepts and making the result circular.

Step 1: Agentic Generation. The agent's first component is an LLM. The LLM does not propose paths directly, but rather path templates. Figure 3 shows the prompt structure. Every configuration receives the same request, 𝑁 req templates under identical beam-search settings. The model is given the target CWE and the binary's label vocabulary, and asked for path templates: a sequence of label subsets rather than of functions. The constraints ensure that the model cannot attribute behavior the binary does not exhibit, and that they are framed as analyst exploration rather than as vulnerability reports, so not every stage needs to be related to the CWE. The prompt allows a model to return fewer templates than requested, so that it is not forced to pad its output with lowquality proposals. The agent then processes the LLM's output using beam search, which searches the binary's call graph for a function carrying each stage's labels, with consecutive stages at most ℎ call edges apart. In real life, an analyst often skips over minor functions in an execution path and focuses on what they deem worthy of more time. We choose ℎ = 3 hops in the call graph to find a middle ground in terms of permissivity. Another common analyst behavior is backtracking while analyzing the codebase; the search takes that into account by allowing transitions in either call direction (down to a callee or back up to a caller). The intuition is that the template, through label subsets, ensures key functions are picked up. It then discards templates it cannot complete. From each realizable template, the agent keeps up to 𝑁 path distinct realized paths. A realized path is a sequence of steps an analyst might take while examining the code in search of a vulnerability. Each step is a function that exists in the binary, at most three hops from its neighbor. It is not required to be an execution path (that is a question for a fuzzer tool), but rather a possible exploration path. The deduplicated realized paths are the generator agent's output and are referred to as 'paths' throughout this paper.

Step 2: Reasoner Verification. The reasoner takes the generated paths as input and executes the domain knowledge as a logic program. The logic program comprises the DKG's facts and mapping rules together with 42 non-ground rules obtained by instantiating a small set of hand-written schemas over the graph's entity-relationentity triples. The rules fall into three families: label propagation, transitive closure, and analyst traversal with step control, of which Table 2 gives one traversal rule and one label-propagation rule. Inference is carried out with PyReason [1], an open-source inference engine for generalized annotated logic that reasons directly over knowledge graphs. Verifying a single step may require several rules. A label-propagation rule may first combine the raw libc labels at one block into a semantic label, then a DK mapping rule lifts that label onto a DKG concept, and a transitive-closure rule chains relations across several hops, before a traversal rule can fire and validate the analyst's move. Because PyReason computes the minimal model of the whole program, the inference is exact rather than a heuristic graph walk. If no combination of rules can validate a step, that step is non-entailed by the domain knowledge. We report the step along with the full reasoning trace (Figure 8). If any one step of a path is non-entailed, the entire path is non-entailed.

div.head: Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup
div.p: We evaluate across three weakness classes-CWE-121 (stack-based buffer overflow), CWE-415 (double free), and CWE-416 (use-afterfree). Standard target binaries (std) are drawn from BinPool [4], a dataset of Debian binaries curated from historical CVEs; it spans 603 CVEs across 89 CWE classes, so the CWEs we target are represented by real compiled programs whose call graphs and libc usage resemble production firmware. Real-world targets (rw) are firmware extracted from deployed medical devices, confidentially provided, and are the targets EntailLLM is required to analyze in our production environment. Table 3 lists the eight binaries behind the results reported here. Ezurio and htmldoc binaries are evaluated for multiple CWEs, making 11 binary-CWE pairs. Sizes span two orders of magnitude, from gpac (405 nodes, 571 edges) to unsafelib (12,696 nodes, 40,881 edges), exercising the pipeline on both small and large call graphs. Agents and Models. The agents are classified by the prompting strategy (zero-shot, chain-of-thought, self-refinement) used. Selfrefinement [16] is a metacognitive strategy [30] in which the model critiques and then revises its own proposals. Then we also separate agents based on whether or not domain knowledge was used to guide the agent a priori. All agents are evaluated with four LLMs in the paper: Opus-4.8, GPT-5.5, Llama 4 Scout, and Kimi K2.5, spanning proprietary and open-weight families. This gives us six agents and a total of 24 configurations per binary-CWE pair. Our initial selection of LLMs also included Claude Fable 5, but its built-in safeguards, which redirect queries on sensitive topics including cybersecurity to a less specialized model, were triggered by our vulnerability-analysis prompts and prevented its use in our agents. Hyperparameters. All LLMs use greedy decoding (𝑡=0.0), since we evaluate each model's most likely output rather than a sample. We request the LLM for 𝑁 req = 50 templates per call, but it had to be lowered to 20 for Llama 4 Scout, whose 8,192-token output cap truncates a 50-template JSON. Paths must span at least six call-graph edges, lowered to four for gpac, whose 405-node graph is too shallow to admit many six-edge paths. Consecutive steps of a path may be up to ℎ = 3 call edges apart (maximum hop distance). The parameter 𝑁 path , the number of realized paths kept per realizable template, was tuned-over {1, 2, 5, 10}: smaller values degraded results and larger ones raised runtime, and LLM cost for no gain, so we use 5. Full settings and rationale are in Appendix. Metrics. #Paths is the number of unique paths an agent outputs. #Entailed gives how many of those the domain knowledge entails, with Entailment% = #Entailed / #Paths × 100. #Paths directly depends on how many templates a model returns and how many of those are realizable. #Entailed can therefore never exceed #Paths, and a low or high number on its own does not reflect the performance. On the other hand, a high entailment% signifies a good result, and a higher #Entailed is desirable alongside it. We tracked template returns for CWE-121 and CWE-416: across these two classes, models returned 53% of the 8,160 templates requested, and 62% of the returned templates were realizable (Appendix). Figure 4 plots #Entailed against Entailment%; The full table for every configuration is in the appendix. An agent-proposed path for which no chain of rule firings can validate every step is a non-entailed trajectory, as the domain knowledge does not support it. When aggregating over configurations we pool #Entailed and #Paths rather than averaging per-configuration percentages, so that generations are weighted by the evidence they carry. Compute. All experiments ran on a single server (AMD EPYC 9755, 128 cores, 754 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04, Python 3.10), with every model accessed through a hosted API (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock). Peak resident memory was ∼21 MB for the generation stage and ∼931 MB for the reasoner, about 0.1% of available RAM, so the pipeline reproduces on commodity hardware.

div.head: Results and Discussion
div.p: Figure 4 shows the effect of domain knowledge on the standard and real-world binaries (top and bottom rows), pooled over all three CWEs. Per-configuration counts are in the Appendix. Domain knowledge improves entailment for both binary types. Pooled entailment increases from 80.9% to 97.7% for standard BinPool binaries and from 71.6% to 98.0% for real-world medical device binaries, and the number of configurations at 100% entailment rises from 22 to 55 and from 17 to 43. We see this in figure 4 as all arrows point upward. Across the 118 configurations where both the unguided and guided agent produced at least one path, entailment improves in 77, is unchanged in 38, and only decreases in 3. A one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test over those 118 paired configurations confirms the shift (𝑊 + = 3180, 𝑊 -= 60, 𝑝 < 10 -13 ; median +8.8 points); the 38 unchanged configurations were already at 100% entailment and are excluded as ties. Separating guidance from verification. A natural concern could be that the guidance labels come from the same graph that the symbolic system uses for reasoning, and whether the +DK setting simply rewards the agent for matching its evaluator. In this neurosymbolic framework, the neural LLM of the agent never trains on the domain knowledge, and the symbols are presented to it only during runtime through the prompt. It has no visibility of the logical rules or the relations in the knowledge graph, which drive the entailment check. Critically, no model is fine-tuned on these labels or on entailment outcomes. That the labels help is therefore an empirical finding, and this work attempts to find an effective way of guiding the neural system. To rule out circularity, we split each knowledge graph into two disjoint halves. Each half keeps every node and edge class. Classes are coarse-grained. For example, labels denoting different types of functions all belong to the same generic class 'functions'. Each half receives only half of the edges of each class. So the two halves share no edges. The split is made on the graph before the reasoner applies the transitive-closure rules, so a half can only infer what its own edges imply. On the three binaries with more than 3,000 call-graph nodes (mupdf-x11, mutool, unsafelib), we run the agents with Opus-4.8 and GPT-5.5, using labels from one half only, and verify each set of paths against the same half and against the other half (tables in the Appendix). If the gain came from the agent seeing its evaluator's facts, paths would be entailed more often by the half that guided them, and the points in Figure 5 would be below and to the right of the diagonal. However, across the 36 comparisons, the mean difference between other-half and same-half entailment is only +0.8 points, and 27 of the 36 points lie within 10% points of the diagonal. This shows that guidance does not unfairly inflate the experimental results, rather, the semantic concepts are a useful tool that can be used to guide the neural component of a neurosymbolic framework. Stability across runs. To check that these gains are not an artifact of a single run, we repeated the full pipeline ten times and measured the spread in entailment across repetitions. As expected, LLM API responses varied, but domain knowledge both raised entailment and sharply narrowed its spread across runs under all three prompting strategies. Results were analogous to a single run. Plots are included in the Appendix.

div.head: EntailLLM Deployment
div.p: EntailLLM is deployed end-to-end inside a vulnerability-discovery pipeline, occupying the solid boxes of Figure 2. A decompiler upstream supplies the labeled call graph; EntailLLM proposes candidate analyst paths over it, checks each against the domain knowledge, and passes only the entailed ones to downstream tooling such as a fuzzer. Results on the three binaries extracted from deployed medical devices are reported in Figure 4 (bottom row). En-tailLLM runs as an interactive web application served from a REST API. The interface mirrors the system's data flow. Figure 1 is a screenshot of the UI showing the graph of an analyzed binary with an agent-proposed path highlighted. Figure 6 shows a snippet of the analyst knowledge graph on the UI. Scalability. Figure 7 shows the scaling capability of the reasoner. Memory remains mostly constant, while runtime scales linearly with steps of reasoning.

div.head: Conclusion and Future Work
div.p: We presented EntailLLM, a neurosymbolic framework that pairs agentic generation of analyst traversal paths through a software codebase with logic-programming verification against domain knowledge. An output path is not merely a plausible traversal of the function call graph according to an LLM-based agent, but provably entailed by the encoded domain knowledge. We examined six agents with four LLMs, for eight binaries and domain knowledge raises pooled entailment from 77.0% to 97.8%, decreasing for only 3 of 118 configurations. This shows the potential of guiding a neural agent with symbolic knowledge. The strongest agent follows a self-refinement prompting strategy guided by domain knowledge, which raises entailment from 71.2% to 97.2% while increasing the number of entailed paths from 1,297 to 1,705. In real-world medicaldevice firmware, in comparison to standard dataset binaries, the entailment rate drops for unguided agents. However, with domain knowledge, rates for both classes of binaries converge. This shows that the system can generalize and the improvements transfer to deployed firmware.

Other than a full report on the deployed system, we plan to extend our work in two directions. First, we plan to include a neurosymbolic corrector module that takes a non-entailed path as an input and attempts to produce a logically entailed alternative with minimal edits. Second, we plan to study the utility of incorporating a cognitive model [3] in our framework. To check that the reported experimental results are not an artifact of a single run, and to establish what entailment rate an uninformed generator would achieve, we repeated the full pipeline ten times for each of the six agents (three prompting strategies, unguided and guided) with each of the four LLMs on two cases: insulininject under CWE-121 and mupdf-x11 under CWE-416. Alongside these we ran ten independent rounds of a No-LLM baseline, in which 25 analyst paths are drawn directly from the binary's call graph, matched to the LLM conditions on path length and on the label-group constraint, so that the only difference is which labels a path visits. No-LLM replaces the LLM's templates with direct path generation over the call graph; no model is involved. Figures 123456show the resulting distributions; all settings are otherwise those of the experimental setup in the main paper.

No-LLM attains 18.0 ± 8.5% entailment on insulininject and 46.4 ± 9.1% on mupdf-x11. Every modelstrategy-combination runs on these two targets exceeds No-LLM under a one-sided Mann-Whitney test against the ten No-LLM rounds (p < 0.05; most at p < 10 -3 ). Pooled over models, the unguided agents sit 57-64 points above No-LLM on insulininject and 32-38 points above on mupdf-x11; with domain knowledge (guided agents) the margins widen to 79-81 and 47-51 points. We make two observations. First, every agent that uses an LLM generates better paths than the No-LLM agent, which forms paths directly from the call graph. Second, Entailment is further improved by the addition of domain knowledge across several runs.

Averaged over the twelve model-strategy combinations per target, the standard deviation of entailment across runs falls from 10.7 to 4.2 on insulininject and from 9.7 to 5.8 on mupdf-x11. The effect is largest where unaided behaviour is least reliable: Kimi K2.5 under self-refinement moves from 54.1 ± 11.3% to 98.3 ± 2.8% on insulininject, and GPT-5.5 under zero-shot from 66.3 ± 9.9% to 99.6 ± 0.8% on mupdf-x11. Several guided agents entail every path in all ten runs, so their spread is zero. Although generation uses greedy decoding, hosted inference APIs are not bit-reproducible; variable request batching perturbs logits enough to flip near-tied argmax decisions, which is the source of the spread reported here.

A run contributes no measurement when the model returns no usable path set. This occurs once in 240 runs on insulininject but in 10.4% of runs on mupdf-x11, and is concentrated in Llama-4 Scout, whose 8,192-token output cap truncates longer responses. Aggregated over all conditions, generation failure accounts for 0% of GPT-5.5 runs, 3.9% of Kimi K2.5, 6.7% of Opus-4.8, and 24.4% of Llama-4 Scout.

div.head: Opus
div.p: Peak memory is flat at roughly 880 MB for every binary because the footprint is dominated by fixed startup costs-the Python interpreter, the JIT-compiled reasoner, and the loaded rules and knowledge graph-all done before any reasoning occurs. The additional memory per time step of reasoning is small by comparison: running six steps instead of one raises peak RSS by at most about 50 MB, about 5% of the baseline, on mupdf-x11. The spread across binaries is small (878-931 MB). For deployment, we note that verification cost scales with trajectory length and with the grounding volume of the binary-DKG pairing, not with the number of trajectories checked, since each is verified independently and the program is restarted after every run. As the memory footprint is dominated by startup, a reasoner process sized for the largest binary is then sized for all of them. The deployment instance of 64 GB (Section 5 of the main paper) has roughly 70× the peak requirement of any single run.

div.head: I.2 Template Generation and Realization
div.p: This section opens up Step 1 of the main paper, the agent's internal stages; the agent's output is the realized paths. A model does not return paths directly: it returns templates, ordered sequences of label subsets, which the agent's beam search must instantiate against the actual call graph. Tables 15 and16 report these counts per configuration for CWE-121 and CWE-416. Of 8,160 templates requested across the two classes, models returned 4,291 (52.6%), of which 2,683 (62.5%) realized as at least one connected chain, ultimately yielding 7,661 unique paths-a mean of 2.86 per realizable template, below the cap of N path = 5 because deduplication removes repeats. Roughly a third of the templates requested, and 62.5% of those a model actually returns, therefore reach the reasoner. The rest is discarded by beam search before any semantic check is applied. Only the request is held fixed across configurations: every configuration asks for the same number of templates under the same beam-search settings. The number of templates returned, the number realizable, and the number of realized paths (#Paths) are all outcomes of the experiment, which is why they differ between configurations. A realized path is a sequence of steps an analyst might take while examining the code, made of functions that exist in the binary and are statically connected in its call graph; it is not an execution path. Domain knowledge is provided before generation rather than on realization. The return rate rises from 46.9% to 58.3% under +DK. So, enrichment makes models propose more.

div.head: I.3 Sensitivity to the Beam-Search Budget
div.p: N path , the number of realized paths kept per realizable template, was the only beam-search parameter tuned. Table 17 repeats the entire CWE-121 evaluation at N path = 10, with every other setting unchanged.

Doubling the budget realizes roughly 1.7× as many paths-4,884 against 2,838 without domain knowledge, and 3,413 against 2,026 with it. But, pooled entailment under +DK is 97.2% at N path = 10 against 98.5% at N path = 5. The effect of domain knowledge is therefore not dependent on how many realizations the beam search retains, and the smaller budget is preferred on runtime and API cost.

div.head: K Deployment: Reasoning Trace Example
div.p: A reasoning trace accompanies every non-entailment inference. A tree recording which observations and which rule firings produced each bound, rooted at the first step the domain knowledge does not entail. Figure 11 shows the trace for the running example of the main paper, in which an agent assigns memset to the memory-management class and then assumes it can perform an integer size calculation.

The leaves are facts of two kinds: libc hasLabel observations on the code blocks along the path (here userInput and scanf), and the stepFrom edges of the proposed trajectory itself, annotated [1,1]. Interior nodes are rule firings. A relation-propagation rule fires on the conjunction of observed labels to derive the higher-level stack based buffer overflow risk label, which is what bridges code-level evidence to the CWE 121 domain-knowledge graph; traversal and step-control rules then advance the analyst along the prefix that the domain knowledge does entail.

At the root, no relation in the domain-knowledge graph connects the labels at the two blocks, so no traversal rule fires and analystAt at that block never reaches µ min . The step-control rule of Section J then makes the corresponding stepFrom bound [0, 0], contradicting the [1, 1] set from the trajectory, and the program reports the conflict as a non-entailment at that step. Because every node records both its bound update and the fact or rule that caused it, an analyst can audit exactly which observations and which rule firings reject the step, rather than receiving an unexplained conclusion.

Green leaves are facts (libc label observations and the trajectory's own stepFrom edges); orange nodes are rule derivations, each annotated with the bound it assigns; the red root is the first step no domain-knowledge relation entails. Each node records the fact or rule responsible for its bound update. Node labels show hackerAt, the name the deployed end-to-end system uses for the analystAt predicate of the main paper.

You reason about which sequences of function behaviors in a binary are relevant to a given software weakness class (CWE), so that code regions worth reviewing can be prioritized for detection and remediation. Your task is to generate realistic code-review paths -ordered sequences of semantic function behaviors an analyst would examine when assessing a binary for a specific weakness type. These paths describe which code a reviewer would inspect during analysis, not necessarily what they would find.

=== USER PROMPT === CWE Information: CWE ID: CWE-416 CWE Name: Use After Free CWE Description: Use After Free -a program continues to use a pointer after the memory it references has been freed, allowing an attacker to control the freed region and influence program behavior or execution.

Exploration Path Framing: Each path represents the exploration journey of a human expert or security researcher navigating through the binary, looking for potential vulnerabilities. Not every stage in the path needs to directly relate to CWE-416 -a human expert would follow interesting code paths, investigate suspicious functions, explore memory management patterns, and sometimes backtrack from dead ends. The path reflects how someone would realistically explore the code, not just the shortest route to a vulnerability. div.head: M Domain Knowledge: Ontology and Graphs
div.p: The domain knowledge is a CWE-focused, code-centric ontology together with a set of instantiated knowledge graphs, one per weakness class. The ontology defines a layered class hierarchy-from concrete Beacons, CodeEntities, CodeOperations and CodePatterns, through FaultConditions and OutcomeLevelFaults, to CWE-level Vulnera-bilityClasses, connected by a fixed set of typed relations (e.g. is a, unsafe variant of, can cause, mitigates).

A central modelling choice is to represent faults as unsafe variants of otherwise-neutral operations: an out of bounds write is an unsafe variant of a generic memory write. Safe and unsafe behaviour therefore coexist in a single graph, and the reasoner can express how missing or incorrect validation turns an ordinary operation into a memory-corruption event. The layering supports reasoning in both directions: forward, from observable beacons up through the class hierarchy to a CWE-level determination, and backward, from a hypothesised classification down to the code-level evidence that would confirm or refute it. The relation-propagation rules of Section J implement exactly this, which is why most relations are instantiated in both directions with asymmetric bounds.

Each graph is populated initially by automated extraction from technical corpora (reverse-engineering manuals, security advisories, man pages), then refined by automated schema validation with targeted semantic review. We treat the resulting graphs as fixed and assumed correct throughout; the extraction and validation of domain-knowledge graphs is a separate problem that this work does not address. The 16 relation types, taken as the union across graphs, are contributes to, can cause, manifestation of, unsafe variant of, involves, implements, validates, may use, derives, possible realization, is a, evidence of, mitigates, required component of, informative component of and incidental component of. CWE-121 uses all 16; CWE-415 and CWE-416 use 14 each, CWE-415 omitting derives and involves and CWE-416 omitting derives and unsafe variant of. Six of the 16 are made transitive by the closure rules of Section J, and six adjudicate analyst steps in the traversal rules.

div.head: N Extended Related Work N.1 LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
div.p: LLMs are increasingly applied to software vulnerability detection across source code, repair, and binaries; recent surveys chart the rapid growth of this area since 2023 and catalogue the models, datasets, and evaluation setups now in use [11]. A recurring finding, however, is that current models are not yet dependable on their own: a comprehensive benchmarking study by Ullah et al. [13] concludes that LLMs cannot yet reliably identify or reason about security vulnerabilities. Work that does report gains typically pairs the LLM with structure rather than trusting it in isolation-LLMxCPG, for example, uses code-property-graph slices to focus an LLM on vulnerability-relevant context [4]. This unreliability is the gap our work targets: rather than treating LLM output as an answer, we treat each proposed analyst path as a hypothesis to be checked against domain knowledge, and we operate on decompiled binaries because source is unavailable for the medical-device firmware we analyse.

div.head: N.2 LLMs for Binary Reverse Engineering
div.p: A fast-growing line of work applies LLMs directly to stripped or decompiled binaries: LLM4Decompile trains models to recover source-like code from assembly [12]; ReSym recovers variable and data-structure symbols from stripped binaries [14]; and DeGPT uses an LLM to refine and explain decompiler output [3]. Most relevant to our setting, an empirical study of human-LLM teaming in reverse engineering shows that LLMs can accelerate analyst comprehension but also mislead when their suggestions go unchecked [1]. These efforts improve the readability or recovered structure of a binary; they do not verify that an analyst's reasoning over that binary is consistent with what is known about the vulnerability class. Our contribution is complementary and sits downstream: we take the recovered call-graph structure and libc labels as input and add a logical verification layer over the analyst paths reasoned on top of them.

div.head: N.3 Logic and Program Analysis for Binary Vulnerability Discovery
div.p: Classical binary vulnerability discovery relies on static analysis and taint tracking. Karonte propagates taint across the multiple binaries of a firmware image to surface insecure interactions, and its authors note that whole-firmware analysis without such cross-binary reasoning produces overwhelming alert volumes [10]. More recently, LATTE couples an LLM with binary taint analysis, automating the taint-propagation and inspection rules that previously required manual expert customisation and reporting new CVEs in real firmware [5]. These systems share our binary-level, source-free setting and our use of domain rules, but their goal is to emit vulnerability alerts via taint propagation. Ours is a different problem: we verify whether an analyst's exploration path is logically entailed by a domain-knowledge graph under a temporal annotated logic, retaining the exploratory structure that alert-only pipelines discard while still steering it toward vulnerabilities. Where LATTE uses the LLM to produce the analysis, we use logic to check the LLM output.

div.head: N.4 Constraining and Verifying LLM Reasoning with Structure
div.p: Because LLM hallucinations are often confident and cannot be caught by probability-based checks, a growing body of work pairs LLMs with symbolic or structured components. Logic-LM translates a problem into symbolic form, solves it with a deterministic solver, and self-refines from solver errors [9]; knowledge-graph-guided methods such as Reasoning-on-Graphs [6] and Graph-Constrained Reasoning [7] constrain LLM reasoning to paths grounded in a KG to reduce hallucination on question-answering benchmarks.

We share the premise that an independent structured layer must gate LLM output, but differ in kind rather than degree. These methods align reasoning to a walk within a single knowledge graph and are evaluated on naturallanguage QA. In our setting the object being verified is a trajectory through the binary's call graph, while the constraints it must satisfy live in a separate domain-knowledge graph, so verification is an alignment between two graphs rather than a walk within one. The temporal, open-world semantics also admit constraints those methods do not model: analyst position is time-indexed, so a step is licensed only at the time point it is proposed, and negation over derived state lets the program assert what the domain knowledge fails to establish rather than only what it establishes (Section J). The target is likewise different-provable, explainable accept/reject inferences in a safety-critical binary domain, rather than answer faithfulness on general benchmarks.

div.head: N.5 Vulnerabilities in Medical-Device Software
div.p: The application domain motivates the entire effort. Connected medical devices -infusion pumps, insulin pumps, pacemakers-run long-lived embedded software that is hard to patch and frequently analysable only as deployed binaries. Large-scale analyses underscore the scale of the problem: a study of over 200,000 infusion pumps found that roughly three-quarters carried known security weaknesses, many tied to years-old, unpatched CVEs [2], and reviews of FDA safety communications document repeated device vulnerabilities with direct patient-safety consequences [8]. This is precisely the regime our system is built for: source-free analysis of the deployed artifact, with a logical guarantee that retained analyst paths are consistent with encoded domain knowledge.

div.head: N.6 Summary
div.p: Unlike prior LLM-for-security work, which treats the model's output as a prediction to be trusted or scored, we treat each trajectory realized from an LLM template as a hypothesis and pose its validation as a formal entailmentchecking problem against domain-knowledge. To our knowledge, this is the first framework to verify LLM-generated exploration paths-as opposed to final answers or natural-language reasoning-using temporal annotated logic.

div.head: J The Complete Logic Program
div.p: The program Π consists of the 42 non-ground rules listed below, reproduced verbatim in PyReason syntax. The head annotation paired minimum bounds ann fn is the annotation function µ pair of the main paper: it assigns the head the componentwise minimum of the bounds satisfied by the body clauses, so a step is never given a confidence higher than its weakest supporting evidence. The same program is shared across all three CWEs; only the knowledge graph the reasoner reasons with changes. Throughout the experiments, we take the minimum admissible bound µ min of the main paper's problem formulation to be [0.25, 1], matching the guard on analystAt(CB1) in the traversal rules: an analyst is considered present at a block if its bound is at least [0.25, 1]. The bounds in the rules below are hand-set design parameters.

div.head: J.1 Analyst-Traversal and
div.p: Step-Control Rules ( 8) The six traversal rules advance the analyst one step per time point (<-1): if the analyst occupies CB1 with lower bound at least 0.25 and the trajectory contains the edge stepFrom(CB1, CB2), the step is entailed whenever some knowledge-graph relation (can cause, contributes to, derives, unsafe variant of, manifestation of, implements) links a label observed on CB1 to a label observed on CB2. The clause thresholds ([0.1, 1] on hasLabel and on the relation, [0.25, 1] on analystAt) act only as gates; the bound assigned to the head is computed by paired minimum bounds ann fn, which recovers the (cause, effect) label pairing imposed by the relation clause. For each grounded relation edge it takes the elementwise minimum of the relation's bound and the hasLabel bounds of the matching labels on the two code blocks, so inference is never mixed across unrelated label pairs, and annotates analystAt(CB2) with the pair attaining the highest lower bound. If no pair meets the threshold, the head retains its default [0, 1], complete uncertainty, and the step is not entailed.

The final two rules make that failure explicit for reporting. future(Y) marks the block one step ahead on the analyst trajectory; if the analyst never reaches there, the negation rule drives stepFrom(X,Y) toward [0, 0], contradicting the trajectory edge asserted at [1,1]. The two formulations converge. The head failing to reach µ min and the resulting bound conflict on stepFrom identify the same step, and is shown in the reasoning trace of Figure 11.
